entries.title: Democrats win the Senate, setting up divided government for remainder of Trump's term
entries.summary: Democrats won by making inroads in several states where they have long struggled, boosted by a challenging political environment for the GOP dominated by voter frustration over high prices.
entries.content:
Democrats win the Senate, setting up divided government for remainder of Trump's term

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democrats have won a majority in the U.S. Senate, according to a tally of race calls by The Associated Press, setting up a new era of divided government after two years of unified Republican control in Washington.

The result gives Democrats a new check on President Trump through the oversight authority that comes with the majority and sets the stage for a long list of investigations that could come to dominate the remainder of his second term.

Democrats secured control of the chamber after Democrat Josh Turek defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa, according to a race call by The Associated Press. The race for control of the House remains too early to call.

The Senate win marked a remarkable turnaround for Democrats, and an electoral disaster for Republicans, who began the year with little expectation that their 53-47 majority was at risk. But with voters frustrated about the cost of living, the GOP was forced to compete in several states that President Trump won by double digits in 2024.

Democrats needed to flip four GOP seats to win back the chamber. They were able to do so with victories in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas and Iowa.

Their wins were boosted by a challenging political environment for the GOP. In addition to concerns about high prices, polls showed many voters upset about the war in Iran, the president's immigration agenda, his tariff policies and perceived corruption in government.

Loading...

In the closing weeks of the election, President Trump took to the campaign trail and implored Republican voters to pretend he was on the ballot. But at a moment when Trump's approval ratings are hovering near historic lows, the argument was not enough to save the GOP majority.

Democrats rode to victory promising that a key focus would be their affordability agenda, but with Trump still in the White House, the party is unlikely to see many of their priorities signed into law.

In an interview with the Pod Force One podcast that was published Monday, Trump addressed the prospect of losing unified Republican control in Washington, saying he would block Democrats' legislation if they take control of Congress.

"I'll become Mr. Veto," Trump said, adding, "and then at some point we'll probably make deals."

Democrats will also still have to work with Republicans on must-pass legislation, including the 12 annual appropriations bills needed to fund the government.

Democrats will have more influence in other areas, namely nominations and oversight.

Senate Republicans have been key to securing confirmations for Trump's Cabinet and judicial nominations, and more nominations were expected in the final two years of his presidency. A Democratic majority now gives the party control over which nominees will get floor votes.

When it comes to investigations, Democrats have signaled an ambitious agenda, with potential inquiries into everything from the independence of agencies such as the Justice Department and Homeland Security, to the business interests of the president and his family.

Losing the majority marks a blow for Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., who set out to frame the stakes of the election in a September floor speech by saying "hard-working Americans would undoubtedly take a back seat" under a Democratic-led Congress. Thune is largely expected to stay on as the top Senate Republican when the new Congress convenes in January.

Across the aisle, Democrats' victory represents a vindication for Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who faced criticism from some progressives early in the president's second term that he was not doing enough to stand up to Trump.

In an October floor speech, Schumer said Democrats were ready to challenge President Trump and Republicans' agenda.

"We are ready to hit the ground running to lower costs, rein in chaos and stop the corruption," Schumer said. "Republicans broke faith with the American people. We know we need to build that trust with the Americans back up, and we will."

entries.title: Democrat Josh Turek wins the Senate seat in Iowa
entries.summary: Democrat Josh Turek has defeated Sen. Ashley Hinson in Iowa, according to a race call by the Associated Press.
entries.content:
Democrat Josh Turek wins the Senate seat in Iowa

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democrat Josh Turek has won the U.S. Senate race in Iowa, according to a race call by The Associated Press. His win ends more than a decade of Republican control of both Senate seats in the state.

Turek, a state representative from Council Bluffs, beat Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson. He flipped one of the country's most competitive U.S. Senate seats, replacing retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst, who announced she would not be seeking a third term last fall.

Loading...

Turek is a two-time gold medalist playing basketball in the Paralympics. He uses a wheelchair due to spina bifida, a condition he says is due to his father's exposure to Agent Orange in the Vietnam War. He was a relatively unknown state lawmaker who beat Zach Wahls, the former state Senate minority leader, to get the Democratic nomination in June.

Loading...

Turek, who calls himself a "prairie populist," campaigned hard on healthcare reform, attacking Hinson for her support of Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which reduces Medicaid spending nationwide by nearly $1 trillion, and claims that Hinson's personal wealth has increased significantly during her time in Washington.

Both Hinson and Turek emphasized their ability as bipartisan lawmakers to try to sway the state's large number of uncommitted voters, but increased their attacks against their opponents, especially as polling data started to indicate a close race.

As President Trump's approval ratings fell, Iowa's race became more competitive. The state's large agricultural industry in particular has been hit hard by Trump's tariffs and increased diesel prices due to the war in Iran. Hinson seemed to walk a fine line with voters, as some Republicans running for office started distancing themselves from Trump. By summer, the race was considered a toss-up.

The race was one of the most expensive in the country. Federal spending data shows that together, the candidates raised more than $30 million. Outside groups contributed more than $100 million to the race, according to Open Secrets.

In the final quarter of the election, Turek significantly outraised his opponent Hinson, a former TV journalist who was considered a rising star in Iowa politics. Hinson was initially considered a front-runner to replace Ernst and received President Trump's endorsement shortly after she announced her candidacy in a state that has voted for President Trump three times. Trump carried Iowa by a 13-point margin in 2024.

entries.title: Democrat David Crowley will be Wisconsin's first Black governor
entries.summary: Democrat David Crowley defeated Republican Congressman Tom Tiffany in a campaign that focused on "lowering costs for working families" and bringing more jobs to Wisconsin.
entries.content:
Democrat David Crowley will be Wisconsin's first Black governor

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democrat David Crowley will be Wisconsin's first Black governor after defeating Republican Congressman Tom Tiffany, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

The Milwaukee County executive's campaign for governor focused on "lowering costs for working families" and bringing more jobs to Wisconsin.

Tiffany's campaign massively outspent Crowley's, but ultimately that spending didn't get the congressman over the finish line.

With endorsements from outgoing Democratic Gov. Tony Evers and former President Barack Obama, Crowley was able to mobilize Democratic voters after narrowly besting democratic socialist Francesca Hong in the primary.

Crowley's razor-thin win over Hong in August capped a tumultuous Democratic primary. Crowley dropped out of the race at one point, endorsing Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, only to re-enter after she withdrew. He scored the endorsement of Evers, a popular Democratic governor, a factor that some credit as a major contributor to his primary win.

Crowley pitched himself as a "deal-maker," who can work across the aisle. Along with Evers and legislative Republicans, he was involved in the push for a bipartisan bill to allow the city of Milwaukee and Milwaukee County to raise their sales tax rates and earn more revenue for their respective governments. Evers said Crowley also played a large role in negotiations on a $500 million deal to upgrade the baseball stadium where the Milwaukee Brewers play and to keep the team in the city through 2050.

Loading...

Tiffany had a fundraising advantage in the gubernatorial race, as three billionaire donors contributed millions to the effort to get him into office. He was endorsed by key Republicans including President Donald Trump, former Wisconsin Gov. Tommy Thompson, and even former Green Bay Packers quarterback Brett Favre.

Meanwhile, ads promoting Crowley touted Trump's historic unpopularity, tied Tiffany to Trump, and argued that Tiffany's votes for Trump's agenda have resulted in costs going up. Crowley also argued that having Tiffany as governor would lead to income tax cuts for his billionaire donors. One Crowley ad proclaimed, "Wisconsin's not for sale, but Tom Tiffany is, and it'll cost ya."

Crowley made defending Medicaid funding and preserving affordable housing central pillars of his platform. The 40-year-old Crowley also talked about his own experience growing up in poverty and with working-class parents who battled substance abuse and mental health issues during the city's crack-cocaine epidemic. He described working his way out of those hardships through education and community organizing jobs, eventually landing in the Wisconsin legislature, and later, the county executive's office.

Crowley said the historic nature of the race — the fact that he will be the state's first Black governor — is not lost on him. "But I'm running to be a governor for all of us," he said at a campaign stop at the Walworth County Fair. "And it doesn't matter what zipcodes you live in, who you love, or where you come from. I want to make sure that we can move our entire state forward."

Maayan Silver is a reporter for WUWM.

entries.title: Adam Hamilton becomes the first Democratic senator from Kansas in nearly a century
entries.summary: Democrat Adam Hamilton beat Sen. Roger Marshall, a fierce loyalist to President Trump, per a race call by the Associated Press.
entries.content:
Adam Hamilton becomes the first Democratic senator from Kansas in nearly a century

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Kansans are sending Democrat Adam Hamilton to the U.S. Senate, the first time they've sent a Democrat to the chamber since 1932.

Hamilton, the pastor of the largest United Methodist church in the country, preached a moderate approach, and emphasized listening to both sides.

President Trump won Kansas with a double-digit margin in each presidential election since 2016. But Kansans also elected a moderate Democrat to the governor's office, then reelected her in that same time period, showing the state is not a Republican stronghold at all levels.

Loading...

Previous Kansas Senate races have been sleepier. Marshall coasted to Washington with a more than 11-percentage-point margin of victory in 2020, despite some predictions for a more competitive race.

But this year's contest ended up being the most expensive in Kansas history, with Hamilton breaking multiple fundraising records.

Hamilton flirted with running as an independent, but decided to run as an "independent-minded Democrat." Supporters worried if he ran as an independent, he'd split the votes with the Democratic candidate and ultimately send Marshall back to Washington.

Andi Welch, from Johnson County, Kansas doesn't always vote for the Democrat on the ballot, but she voted for Hamilton on Election Day.

"I think he's going to be fair," Welch said. "I think he's running as a Democrat for the reasons he states, and I think he really is going to be looking out for Kansas citizens."

Hamilton's call for term limits, critiques of national Democrats and endorsements from prominent Kansas Republicans resonated with Kansans.

Loading...

But the race also delved into personal attacks.

The New York Times reported that Marshall, who worked as an OB-GYN before being voted to the U.S. House in 2016, sued 700 of his former patients for medical debt. Hamilton's campaign used one of those former patients in an attack ad, and five days before Election Day that patient sued Marshall for allegedly charging a predatory interest rate.

Marshall's campaign, for its part, bet heavily on an attack ad surrounding claims that Hamilton protected a pedophile. A church camp volunteer reportedly attempted to sexually abuse boys at one of Hamilton's church camps, and returned the following year where he did so again.

Court records show the church's initial investigation into the boys' report was inconclusive, and Hamilton later said in a debate he was not involved in the decision to allow the volunteer to return. Church leaders called the authorities after the second report, but Hamilton said they should've called police after the first.

National Republicans also turned their focus to the state, betting that the remaining undecided voters — which made up about 8% of the electorate in September, according to an Emerson College poll — were Trump voters who just needed encouragement to get out and vote. The president and vice president each visited the state twice this election season.

Still, polls trended in Hamilton's favor — Emerson's by a wider margin than before their visits.

Hamilton notably avoided association with national Democrats, which aligns with his "independent-minded" Democrat stance. Though his campaign took $5 million from a political action committee associated with U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Hamilton said he wouldn't support Schumer for another leadership position.

In their final debate before Election Day, Marshall sought to tie Hamilton to Schumer 15 times.

Hamilton, meanwhile, leaned into a Kansas-first approach, a message that appealed to voters.

entries.title: Missourians reject ballot proposal that would have re-imposed an abortion ban
entries.summary: Missouri voters defeated a measure that would have banned abortion just two years after voters legalized abortion in another vote. Voters in Missouri legalized abortion two years ago but this time the abortion ban was coupled with a ban on transgender treatment for minors. Opponents said it was misleading.
entries.content:
Missourians reject ballot proposal that would have re-imposed an abortion ban

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

St. Louis, MO – Missouri voters defeated a proposal to ban abortion, according to a race call by the Associated Press. It reaffirms the vote they took in 2024 that lifted one of the country's strictest abortion bans.

The proposal had been placed on the ballot by the Republican-led legislature and it would have banned abortion except in the case or rape and incest for the first 12 weeks of pregnancy or longer for fetal anomalies.

Its defeat was a major victory for the state's abortion rights supporters. It maintains the state's current law, allowing abortion until fetal viability, though there are restrictions on how they're performed.

Missouri is one of four states that had abortion on the ballot. Since the Supreme Court struck down federal protections for abortion rights in 2022, abortion law has become a state-by-state patchwork across the country.

The defeat also sent a message of voter support for transgender rights. After losing on an abortion ban two years ago, abortion opponents coupled this proposal in a single question with a ban on puberty blockers, hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery for minors.

Loading...

Prominent Republican leaders, including Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe, raised money and campaigned to pass the abortion ban. But many of the ads supporting the proposal didn't mention abortion but focused on the gender affirming care ban. Opponents of abortion rights defended the strategy, contending that part of the initiative was popular with voters.

"I think that the abortion issue is much closer to a 50/50 issue in the state, as is evidenced by what happened in 2024," Republican state Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick had said. "Whereas the issue of trans medical [procedures] is probably more like an 80/20 issue."

Abortion rights proponents saw the focus on gender affirming care as an attempt at misdirection. They also pointed out that gender affirming care for minors is already banned in Missouri through statute, though the prohibitions on puberty blockers and hormone therapy expire in 2027.

The campaign committee angling to defeat the proposal, called Amendment 3, also had a monetary advantage. It received more than $26 million in donations of $5,000 or more since the beginning of the year, compared to around $6.7 million worth of large donations for the campaign trying to pass the abortion ban.

Jason Rosenbaum covers politics for St. Louis Public Radio.

entries.title: Democrat Gina Hinojosa wins race for Texas governor, ousting Greg Abbott
entries.summary: Hinojosa, an Austin state representative, is set to be the state's first Democratic governor since 1995 and will be the state's first Latina governor.
entries.content:
Democrat Gina Hinojosa wins race for Texas governor, ousting Greg Abbott

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott ending more than three decades of Republican control of the Texas governor's office, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

The victory denies Abbott a fourth term and elevates an Austin state representative who built her campaign around public education, household costs and criticism of the state's Republican leadership.

When Hinojosa, 52, takes office in January 2027 she will be the first Latina sworn in to serve as Texas governor and the first Democratic governor since Ann Richards, who left office in 1995.

A former Austin school board president who grew up in the Rio Grande Valley, Hinojoas built her campaign around public education and household costs.

Loading...

She opposed the private-school voucher program championed by Abbott that began in 2026 with $1 billion in tax money for students attending private schools. She pledged to replace Texas Education Commissioner Mike Morath, a software developer and investor, with an educator.

Abbott, 68, promised to lower property taxes in the state and said he had made Texas safer, in part by securing the border.

David Crockett, a political science professor at Trinity University in San Antonio, said before the election that a win by Hinojosa "would be perceived as an earthquake" after decades of Republican statewide victories.

But she'll likely face a Republican-led legislature. "Getting any meaningful legislation through is going to require them to find something they can agree on and that's not going to be easy," Crockett said.

Nancy Sims, a political science lecturer at the University of Houston, said before Election Day that a Democratic breakthrough would reflect frustration with Washington.

"If Democrats win in Texas in 2026, it will be because of anger at the federal government and at Donald Trump," she said.

entries.title: Democrat Rob Sand wins Iowa governor's race, ending GOP control of the office
entries.summary: Democratic State Auditor Rob Sand stressed affordability and often talked about how his Christian faith guides him.
entries.content:
Democrat Rob Sand wins Iowa governor's race, ending GOP control of the office

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democratic State Auditor Rob Sand defeated Republican businessman Zach Lahn in Iowa's race for governor, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

Voters chose the two-term state auditor, electing a Democrat for the first time since Chet Culver in 2006. Republicans have held the office since 2011. Sand will succeed Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds, who decided not to seek another term.

Sand's victory marks a shift in a state that has moved toward the GOP. President Donald Trump carried Iowa by more than 13 percentage points in 2024. Trump endorsed Lahn.

Sand, 44, was a notable exception. In 2022, he narrowly won reelection as auditor, becoming the only Democrat to hold statewide office. He's stood out as a Democrat who has talked for years about how his Christianity informs his policy, sometimes saying in his campaign, "Jesus is for the little guy."

Before becoming state auditor, he was an assistant attorney general who led the investigation and prosecution of the largest lottery-rigging scheme in U.S. history, involving manipulated jackpots across five states.

He ran on government accountability and cooperation across party lines. Education was a major dividing line. Sand criticized Iowa's education savings account, or voucher, program, which uses public money to help families pay private school tuition. He called for greater investment in public schools.

Loading...

Lahn defended the program saying parents deserve more choices in their children's education.

Sand also campaigned on affordability and expanding access to health care, calling for an end to Medicaid privatization.

The governor's race was expensive. Campaign finance reports covering mid-July through mid-October showed the candidates spent more than $46 million. Sand accounted for about $29 million of that spending.

Lahn raised slightly more during that period, with most of his cash contributions coming from the Republican Governors Association's Right Direction PAC. Sand also received millions from the Democratic Governors Association.

Lahn, a first-time candidate, emphasized his business experience. He previously worked for Americans for Prosperity, a conservative advocacy group associated with the Koch family, and co-founded Wonder, a private school in Wichita, Kansas.

Both candidatesraised concerns about water quality and Iowa's high cancer rates. The state has the nation's second-highest rate of new cancer diagnoses.

He takes office in January, but advancing his agenda will require working with a Republican-controlled Legislature. The GOP holds majorities in both the Iowa House and Senate.

Sheila Brummer reports for Iowa Public Radio.

entries.title: Missouri voters turn down a Republican-backed congressional map
entries.summary: Missouri voters have denied a Republican-backed congressional map that wound its way through the courts before ultimately ending up on the state's ballot.
entries.content:
Missouri voters turn down a Republican-backed congressional map

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Missouri voters have denied a Republican-backed congressional map that wound its way through the courts before ultimately ending up on the state's ballot. That's according to a race call by the Associated Press.

Loading...

GOP lawmakers in Missouri had passed the map last year to try to oust Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver by redrawing his Kansas City district. The goal was to pick up an additional House seat for Republicans.

The new district lines came amid a national mid-decade redistricting rush that was initiated by President Trump to try to boost his party ahead of the midterm elections.

Missouri's top court ruled that the Republican-backed map could not be in effect for the midterms, and instead voters would get to decide on it. The U.S. Supreme Court upheld that state court ruling.

Cleaver easily won reelection Tuesday, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

Missouri is not the only state deciding ballot measures relating to redistricting.

Maryland voters approved a constitutional amendment to change rules for congressional redistricting, allowing Democratic state leaders to redraw districts ahead of the 2028 election.

And Colorado voters are deciding a constitutional amendment that would ban congressional maps that purposefully favor one political party.

entries.title: Democrat Sherrod Brown wins Ohio Senate race
entries.summary: Democratic former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown has won back a seat on Capitol Hill, defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted after a close and expensive battle, according to a race call by the Associated Press.
entries.content:
Democrat Sherrod Brown wins Ohio Senate race

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democratic former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown has won back a seat on Capitol Hill, defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted after a close and expensive battle, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

Brown is the seventh former U.S. senator since 1946 to lose his seat and then return to the Senate later.

Loading...

After serving three terms, he was defeated by Bernie Moreno in 2024 in what the ad tracking site AdImpact ranked as the most expensive non-presidential election on record at the time (that honor now goes to this year's Senate race in Texas).

This was Husted's first race for the U.S. Senate. He was appointed to the seat by Gov. Mike DeWine in January 2023 after JD Vance won the vice presidency. But Husted has had a long career in elected office in Ohio, serving as speaker of the Ohio House, the secretary of state and lieutenant governor.

Ohio has been a Republican stronghold for years, with President Trump winning Ohio in the last three presidential cycles. But because of Brown's name recognition, polls showed the race was close all year, and it got more attention amid building signs of a national "blue wave" for Democrats.

The campaign started quietly, with neither Brown nor Husted doing a splashy launch. Both leaned toward smaller events at first, but joined big rallies that came up in the last month.

Loading...

Brown was part of a rally led by former President Barack Obama on Oct. 24. And Husted met up with Trump in his three visits to Ohio in October, and became one of several male office-seekers who earned odd praise from Trump on their physiques.

Data centers, affordability, the war in Iran and health care costs were major issues in the campaign. Brown had made data centers a key talking point, calling Husted "the face of data centers" in Ohio because of his involvement with such deals when he was lieutenant governor. A leaked memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee defined data centers as "the anchor hanging around Husted's neck" and suggested if Husted lost, it would affect future races around the country. (NPR hasn't independently confirmed the authenticity of the memo.)

Brown far outraised Husted, with the candidates together bringing in more than $80 million. Ohio was the only state with a close U.S. Senate race where Democrats had more broadcast TV ads than Republicans, according to AdImpact. As of mid-October, the candidates and outside groups had spent more than $422 million, making this race one of the most expensive U.S. Senate contests in the country.

Brown is assured of only two more years in the U.S. Senate. Because this year's election was to fill the rest of the term Vance was elected to in 2022, Brown will have to run for reelection in 2028 to keep the seat.
